A1. Stream Drainage Systems
A1.1. Stream Drainage System Formation
Streams begin when water reaches land. They begin flowing as a thin, uniform flow, or a sheetwash, but then divide into tiny channels. These are called “rills.” The channels grow longer and deeper uphill during headward erosion (shown on the right) Eventually, these channels merge into a drainage network, called a stream  drainage system. 
A1.2. Stream Drainage System Types
A drainage system type can depend on the rock type that it develops on. There are three types of drainage systems:

Dendritic drainage patterns are the most common. They look like a natural tree with lots of branches, and develop on a land surface where the rock underneath is uniformly hard. In other words, it resists erosion the same amount. It is shown to the right. One example is the Mississippi river. 
Radial drainage patterns develop in weird circle shapes? They develop in “pointy” areas, like a volcano or a hill. One example is Mount fuji, or Mount rainer.
Centripital drainage patterns are the opposite of radial. They develop in areas that look like bowls, where water from surrounding high areas flow into the centre.  Dead Sea or Great Basin would be an example of this. 
Rectangular drainage patterns look like…well…like dendritic drainage patterns but rectangular. They develop when weaker rocks form in a rectangular fashion, causing the running water to break down the weaker rock. Vindyhan Mountains in india is an example of this. 
Trellis drainage patterns develop in regions where there is a river running through a region of alternating hard and soft rock. Following the path of least resistance, water travels in streams in regions of soft rock, forming an interesting system. An example could be the appalachian valley. 
Deranged drainage patterns start out as one of the top 4 drainage patterns, but then get disrupted. This can happen via a variety of causes, most notably glacial activity, tectonic disturbances, volcanic eruptions, or mass landslides. An example could be the canadian shield in…c-c-c-ca-ca-cambodia!
A1.3. Stream Order Definitions
Stream Order  is a ranking system that shows the relative size and complexity of streams in a river system.
It can be measured in multiple different systems. The most common in the Strahler Stream Order (1957), shown to the right. Independent streams that have no connected streams before have a magnitude of 1. When two streams connect and merge with magnitude A and B, the resulting stream has a magnitude of the maximum of A and B.  When two streams of the same order join, they create a stream of one higher order. While this provides an approximation for discharge and such. However, this  does not account for all streams. Lower-ordered streams can be ignored when merging with higher-order streams.
Depending on what magnitude a stream is, we can infer some stuff about it!
The Shreve Stream Order (1966) is similar to the Strahler Stream Order. However, the main difference is that when two streams of order A and B join together, the resulting stream has an order of A+B. Although this is a more direct reflection of network size and discharge than Strahler, though it is not designed to braided  rivers and such.
Finally, the Hack’s Stream Order  (1957) works very differently. The main channel (A2), is given an order of 1, and any streams that feed into it,  also known as tributaries, have an order of one higher than the distributary it fed into. One weakness this has, however, is that it treats  all streams of the same order the same, discharge and such cannot be inferred. However, a stream’s relationship to its main trunk can now be easily filtered. 
A Headwater Stream is the very beginning, or source, of a stream or river system. These are typically small, and are 1st or 2nd order streams in the Strahler system.
A  Middle Reach Stream is the middle of a stream or river system. These are usually the 3rd-5th order streams in the Strahhler system.
A Lower Reach Stream is  typically near the mouth of  a stream, with  a 5th order or higher.
The stream with the highest Strahler Stream Order is the Amazon River, with an order of 12. Second place is the Mississippi River, with an order of 10. Third place goes to the Congo River (Africa), Volga River (Europe), Columbia River (US), and the Ganges River  (Asia) all with an order of 9.TODO: Organize this junk
The stream with the highest Shreve  Stream  Order is, again, the Amazon River, with an order of over hundreds of thousands. Second Place is the Congo River, with a Shreve Order of 150,000+. Third place is the Mississippi river, with  100,000+. 
The Bifurcation Ratio is a magical and wonderful thing ✨.  It is the ratio of the number of streams with one order to the number of streams of the next higher order. Usually, this number stays constant for all orders, and a stream’s bifurcation number says something about that stream. If a bifurcation number is below 3, it means that a stream is low branching, possibly because of structural control or an elongated basin. If it is above 5, then it is highly branched, possibly because of rough terrain or impermeable surfaces. A normal bifurcation ratio would be between 3 and 5, and a “perfect” one would be 4, according to Horton’s “law of stream numbers.”

A4.  Stream Channel Pattern
A4.1 Straight Channel Pattern
A Straight Channel Pattern is…well…straight. It usually has either a very high or very low slope. They usually have a low sediment load, and have very strong banks usually made of bedrock. However, they are usually very rare in nature, and when they do appear, they are usually very short. They could appear via: fault lines, bedwork gorges, or human-made canals. 
A4.2 Meandering Channel Pattern
A Meandering Channel looks kinda like a snake, going back and forth. It develops in areas of low slope, and has a fine sediment load, consisting of silt and sand. It has sticky, cohesive banks 
Composed of clay or rooty soil. They have a steady flow. 

They form in 5 steps. 1. A straight channel deepens. 2. The river begins to oscillate, undercutting the outer bank, and depositing sediment at the inside of the bend, or point bar. 3. Abrasion deepens the channel, point bars form on the inside of banks. 4. Helicoidal Flow begins creating bends. 5. Erosion progresses forward.

You might be curious, what is Helicoidal Flow, also known as the corkscrew motion? It is the spiral-pattern movement of water in meandering river bends. When water enters a meander bend, it piles up on the outside, splashing down due to gravity. Due to pressure, the water moves towards the inside, it resurfaces and, because of centrifugal force, goes back to the outside.

To put in simpler terms, it forms when a slightly curvy straight channel pattern, like the one shown above, gradually changes over time when the outside of the bend, or the cut bank, erodes due to faster waters, and the inside of the band, or the point bar, deposits due to slower waters. 

Some more vocabulary: a meander loop is one of the many u-bends that a meandering channel does. When a meander loop is cut off from the meandering channel, it is called an Oxbow lake. A meander neck is the length of the “hole” in a meander loop. A meander neck cutoff is when the meander neck closes and forms a more efficient route for the water to pass through. This may result in a meander scar, an empty channel, a trace of the dead  meandering channel. Similar to the meander neck cutoff, the meander chute cutoff can happen across a point bar, and usually happens during floods. See image on right.
















A4.3 Braided Channel Pattern
A Braided Channel look like a normal river, except there are a bunch of islands in the middle of them. appears in moderate to steep slopes, with very high coarse sediment loads, including sand, gravel, and cobbles. They have weak and easily eroded banks, and highly variable discharge due to flashy floods. They form like this: during a flood, a river carries lots of sediment. When the flood ends, the sediment drops, mostly in the middle, forming a small weak island due to deposition, also called Braid Bars.  Because braided channels form in weak areas, they are very unstable.
Some niche vocab (NICHE REFERENCE!!!): when a channel cuts across a bar, it is called a Chute. Each individual flowing channel in a braided channel is called a thread. 
Braided channels are most commonly found in glacial outwash plains, mountain streams with landslide debris, deserts after flash floods, and rivers downstreams of volcanos.  It should also be noted these form quickly, less than a century.

A4.4 Anastomosing Channel
An Anastomosing Channel 	is very similar to braided in terms of look, but in reality is quite different. For one, its island has life, and are much more stable. The entire thing, in fact, is much more  stable. The channels are all very stable, and there is very little sediment. The sediment is fine, consisting of silt and clay, and rather than a mode rate to steep climate, it develops in a very gentle slope. It has very strong banks, consisting of clay or roots. It moves slow rather than fast, and it usually develops on lowland deltas, swampy plains, and large rivers. 
Here is how they form: they form in extremely strong banks. Thus, when something blocks the river’s flow, the water rises up and flows over the blockage, forming a new path not necessarily in the same position as the old path. This process of abandoning an original path in favor of a new one is called an anabranch in a process called avulsion. The result is an island in the middle of a stream, but this time much stronger and vegetable-filled. It should be noted these form very slowly; in thousands of years.

A Wandering Channel is a combination of a meandering and braided channels, and actually shown above. An intermediate slope, and a combination of coarse and fine sediment is required, as well as a moderate bank strength. It forms the same way as meandering, but forms bars occasionally. That  is, it is a ratio between the total length of a stream, and the absolute length from the beginning to the end. For example, a river that is perfectly straight would have a sinousity of 1, while a meandering river  might have a sinuosity of 3.

A5. Sediments

Bedload, which are coarse particles like sand, gravel, cobbles. These move by rolling, sliding, or bouncing along the bottom, a process called saltation. These usually carry about 5-25% of the total load.
Suspended load, which are fine particles like silt, clay, sand. These are carried by the water and kept up by turbulence. The largest particle size a stream can move is called competence, while the finest sediment that is in the suspended load is called the wash load. The total load a stream can carry is called capacity.  These usually carry around 60-90% of the total load. 
Dissolved load, which are ions like calcium, bicarbonate, and sodium. These are carried with the water, because they are dissolved in them. These come from chemical weathering of rocks, and are in high concentrations in limestone regions, and lower in granite.

A6. Stream Flow
A6.1 Perennial/Intermittent/Ephemeral streams
Perennial/Significant streams are streams that are present year-round. This is usually due to being connected to groundwater via baseflow (see A6.2).
Intermittent streams that are present part of the year. These are usually due to having seasonal discharge inflow stuff, like snow melt or other stuff. 
Ephemeral streams are streams that are absent unless precipitation exists. 
A6.2 Gaining & Losing Streams
Gaining streams, or a fluent stream receive water from groundwater surrounding, while losing streams, or an influent stream lose water. What determines this gain/loss is the hydraulic head, or how fast water is moving in a place. Water that has more pressured always goes towards lower pressured waters. This is called baseflow.  Because a stream gains water as it moves downstream, its discharge increases. On the other hand, losing streams will eventually die out because the groundwater steals all its water :O
A6.3 Calculating the Discharge
To calculate discharge, you have to know the cross sectional area and the velocity. Usuually, the cross-section of a river is split into 25 to 30 rectangles, like a riemann sum, and the depth and velocity is found for each rectangle. Then, the depth, velocity, and riemann thingy width are multiplied together to get the discharge of a segment. The discharges of all the segments are added together to find the total discharge. Why do we have to do this cat and mouse chase you ask? Well, velocity and depth vary. That’s right! Velocity in rivers are the highest in the center, assuming there are no bends or other willy wonky thingies. 
In order to find the velocity, a current meter can be used. It has a wheel, that turns when water pushes it, and converts that into a number. Simple. The most common type of current meter is a Price AA Current meter. 6 buckets revolve around a center axis, and the rate of revelusion is turned into velocity. It is also designed to be attached to a wading rod in shallow waters, or mounted above a weight suspended above a cable in deeper waters. It should be noted that in shallow waters, a Pygmy Price Current Meter, a 2/5th version of a price AA, is used instead. 
There is also the float method: Measure how long a floating object takes to travel a certain distance, and use that to calculate the surface velocity. Then, multiply it by a factor because surface water moves faster than bottom water. This number is roughly 0.9 if the bed is smooth, and roughly 0.8 if the bed is rocky. This is a backup method for using a current meter, though it is less accurate.
Now, on to depth. You remember the wading rod from before? It is used to find depth in shallow, calm waters. A person sticks the wading rod, which is like a really long meterstick (METRIC SYSTEM RULES), into the water and reads the label. If the water is too fast or deep, a sounding weight is used instead. It is a weight on a copper wire fishing rod. A person fishes out the fishing rod weight, and reels it lower until they feel impact. They then see how much cable they used, and that is the depth :D. This happens off a boat, of course.

A8. Floods
Floods are caused by sudden and plentiful water, possibly caused by heavy rainfall or prolonged storms, rapid snowmelt. Urbanization, saturated soil, steep terrain, and lack of vegetaion could further worsen flooding.

A flood can be described as a N-year flood. This N can be calculated by the following formula: if a stream has Y years of data. Then the Kth largest flood has a reccurence interval, or N, of (Y+1)/K. A recurrence interval of N does not mean a flood would occur once every N years. Rather, it means a flood has a 1/N probability of occurring each year.

A10. River Deltas
A10.1 Delta Definition & Formation
A river delta is a depositional landform that forms at a river’s mouth when it flows into a slower body of water, like an ocean, sea, or lake. The sudden drop in water velocity causes sediment to be  dropped, causing salt, silt, and clay to be dropped. This creates  a fan, triangular, or bird’s foot shape. A delta will form if river deposition happens faster than wave, tide, or currents can erode it away.
It  forms in 5 steps
River erodes sediment and begins transporting it
The velocity off the water carrying the sediment plummets as it reaches standing  water
It deposits, sorting itself by size before sinking.
Sediment buildup creates a bar, a chunk of land that splits  teh channel water into separate  channels
This process repeats, leading to progradation where the delta slowly grows seaward over time
A10.2 Delta Anatomy
All deltas can be split into three main parts:
The upper delta plain is located above the water. Meaning, even at high tide the  upper delta plain stays above water. It can contain freshwater marshes, swamps, and shallow lakes.
The lower delta plain sits in the middle and is flooded by tides during high tides. It features slightly salty bays and mangrove swamps.
The subaqueous, or underwater, delta lies completely below the water and forms a platform of which the rest of a delta is built. 
Some more vocabulary:
A delta plain is the combination of the upper and lower delta plains. A delta front is the steep, sloping area that faces the open water. The prodelta is the farthest zone where the smallest of the smallest of the particles can settle.
A10.3 River/wave-dominated Deltas
A river-dominated delta forms where wave forces are weak. In turn, the shape of the delta is controlled mostly by the river, resulting in a  very outward, irregular outline. One example is the Mississippi river, with a bird’s foot shaped delta shown on the right.
A wave-dominated delta forms when  wave forces are strong. Thus,  waves control the delta, creating a classic fan or arc shape. The Nile  River   is an example of this.

A11. Alluvial Fans
A11.1 Formation
Alluvial fans are large cone or fan-shaped piles of sediment such as gravel, sand, or silt that forms when a steep mountain stream suddenly goes into a flat valley floor. 
When a fast-moving stream rushes down a mountain canyon and hits the wide, flat valley floor, also called the mountain front, their velocity decreases drastically, by around 90%. Meaning, some heavy sediment such as gravel or sand that was previously transported or even eroded are not deposited, depositing huge amounts of sand and gravel.
The best place to see alluvial fans is Death Valley, because the mountains are steep, the valley is flat, and there are rare desert thunderstorms. No vegetation or rivers to erode them away as well.
A11.2 Anatomy
The apex is the highest point of the fan, located at the mouth of the canyon. This is where the biggest, heaviest sediment that really can’t go that far are deposited. The mid-fan is where medium-sized gravel and sand is deposited. Water flowing through here can form braided streams. The toe (THEORY OF EVERYTHINGGGG) of a fan is where the finest sediments such as silt and clay are deposited.
Finally, an incision is when a stream cuts a deep channel in its own fan, meaning instead of the water spreading out and going everywhere it goes through the channel.

A11. Waterfalls
A11.1 Anatomy and Formation 
How are waterfalls formed? When a stream passes through a bank of resistant rock called a caprock, and then a bank of softer rock, the softer rock erodes quicker, creating a height difference in the water above the hard rock and the water above the soft rock. The line where water thus falls is called the fall line, and the point on the stream where  the water falls is called a lip/knickpoint. A plunge pool is formed by the force of the falling water, which carves a basin at the bottom. The water undercuts the soft rock, forming a small hollow cave called  a rock shelter/grotto at the base beneath the hard rock, which eventually collapses, forming a talus/scree.  Then, the cycle repeats again and again as the fall line moves upstream. This  leaves behind a steep-sided, narrow valley called a “gorge.”
Because the speed of water increases near a waterfall, the rock near a waterfall can be very smooth due to higher amounts of erosion. 
This is  not the only way they can form, however.

D2. Thermal Stratification and Mixing
D2.1 Lake Layers
During the summer, a lake splits  into 3  layers that do not  mix. 
The topmost layer is called the Epilimnion. This is  the warm,  sunny surface water at the top.
The middle layer is called the Metalimnion is the sharp decrease in temperature, known as the thermocline.
The lowest layer is called the Hypolimnion, is the cold, dark, and dense water at the bottom. 
You can find more info at D5.1 Lake Regions.
D2.2  Thermal Mixing Patterns
There are many types of lakes that mix in different durations…yeah let’s just begin.
Dimictic Lakes mix two times a year. During the summer, a hot Epilimnion is formed on the surface while a cold Hypolimnion is formed at the bottom. 
During the fall, as autumn air cools the surface water, it becomes denser and sinks. This eventually destroys the thermal cline, and winds easily mix the lake from top to bottom. 
During the winter, water freezes and an ice layer floats on the top. Below, a cold layer of water below 4 degrees celsius floats above the warmer water below.
During the spring, the ice thaws and the  lake  is now uniform in temperature. Winds thus easily push the  entire water column, and the lake mixes completely from  top to bottom. 
Polymictic Lakes mix very often. They are shallow lakes, typically less than  15-20 feet deep, located in temperate or tropical environments. 
Cold polymictic lakes appear in very cold  areas, in which frozen, shallow lakes thaw during the summer and mix really easily with the wind.  Warm polymictic lakes appear in tropical or warm regions, where the sun heats  the entire shallow water column evenly every day, and night  cooling makes the surface cooler and thus denser, and thus turning over the lake. 
Amictic Lakes never mix. These are permanently ice-covered  lakes, found in places like Antarctica or the Arctic.
Meromictic Lakes never fully mix. They are chemically stratified, usually because the deep water is much saltier, therefore denser,  than the surface water.  They can form in arid climates where evaporation concentrates salts, or deep sinkholes or volcanic craters where salty groundwater  seeps in at the bottom. 
Monomictic  Lakes mix one time a year. There are cold and warm monomictic lakes.
Warm monotonic lakes  occur in warm climates, in which  the thermocline is very thin such that during the winter, the coldness is just enough such that it can mix.  Cold ones are the opposite.

 Climatic Drying. If  a region dries for a long period of  time, the lake’s water can  evaporate faster than its source can regenerate is. As such, the lake shrinks and withers away.

D5.1 Thermal  Stratification Zones
[COPIED FROM D2.1] During the summer, a lake splits  into 3  layers that do not  mix. 
The topmost layer is called the Epilimnion. This is  the warm,  sunny surface water that is  usually  18-26 celsius. It  is  heated by the  sun and wind, and because warm water is less dense, it floats on top of the denser cold water of the bottom layers. 
The middle layer is called the Metalimnion, also known  as the thermocline. This is the layer in which there is a rapid or sharp decrease in  temperature, often by 7-8  celsius per meter. This thermocline is the reason  why the topmost layer can mix with the bottom ones
The bottommost layer is called the Hypolimnion, is the cold, dark, and dense water at  the bottom, hovering at around  3-5 celsius. It is an oxygen-deprived “dead zone” because it receives no oxygen from the surface due to the thermal stratification, and whatever oxygen WAS down  there was used up by the decomposing organic matter.

Life  here are heterotrophs, meaning they must consume food or decaying matter. Organisms include: lake trout, whitefish, crayfish, and organisms that feed on “marine snow”.

Trellis drainage patterns develop in regions where there is a river running through a region of alternating hard and soft rock. Following the path of least resistance, water travels in streams in regions of soft rock, forming an interesting system. An example could be the appalachian valley. Deranged drainage patterns start out as one of the top 4 drainage patterns, but then get disrupted. children.label: A1.3 Stream Order Definitions
children.description: Stream Order  is a ranking system that shows the relative size and complexity of streams in a river system. It can be measured in multiple different systems. The most common in the Strahler Stream Order (1957), shown to the right. Independent streams that have no connected streams before have a magnitude of 1. When two streams connect and merge with magnitude A and B, the resulting stream has a magnitude of the maximum of A and B.  When two streams of the same order join, they create a stream of one higher order. While this provides an approximation for discharge and such. However, this  does not account for all streams. Lower-ordered streams can be ignored when merging with higher-order streams. Depending on what magnitude a stream is, we can infer some stuff about it! The Shreve Stream Order (1966) is similar to the Strahler Stream Order. However, the main difference is that when two streams of order A and B join together, the resulting stream has an order of A+B. Although this is a more direct reflection of network size and discharge than Strahler, though it is not designed to braided  rivers and such. Finally, the Hack’s Stream Order  (1957) works very differently. The main channel (A2), is given an order of 1, and any streams that feed into it,  also known as tributaries, have an order of one higher than the distributary it fed into. One weakness this has, however, is that it treats  all streams of the same order the same, discharge and such cannot be inferred. However, a stream’s relationship to its main trunk can now be easily filtered. A Headwater Stream is the very beginning, or source, of a stream or river system. These are typically small, and are 1st or 2nd order streams in the Strahler system. A  Middle Reach Stream is the middle of a stream or river system. These are usually the 3rd-5th order streams in the Strahhler system. A Lower Reach Stream is  typically near the mouth of  a stream, with  a 5th order or higher. The stream with the highest Strahler Stream Order is the Amazon River, with an order of 12. Second place is the Mississippi River, with an order of 10. Third place goes to the Congo River (Africa), Volga River (Europe), Columbia River (US), and the Ganges River  (Asia) all with an order of 9.TODO: Organize this junk The stream with the highest Shreve  Stream  Order is, again, the Amazon River, with an order of over hundreds of thousands. Second Place is the Congo River, with a Shreve Order of 150,000+. Third place is the Mississippi river, with  100,000+. The Bifurcation Ratio is a magical and wonderful thing ✨.  It is the ratio of the number of streams with one order to the number of streams of the next higher order. Usually, this number stays constant for all orders, and a stream’s bifurcation number says something about that stream. If a bifurcation number is below 3, it means that a stream is low branching, possibly because of structural control or an elongated basin. If it is above 5, then it is highly branched, possibly because of rough terrain or impermeable surfaces. A normal bifurcation ratio would be between 3 and 5, and a “perfect” one would be 4, according to Horton’s “law of stream numbers.”

Usually, a wide and shallow channel means easily eroded banks and lots of sediment, while a deep and narrow channel means resistant banks, little sediment, and high flow energy. children.label: A3 Hydrographs
children.description: Hydrographs measure a stream’s discharge, volume of water per second, changes over time. Like every mathy graph, it has lots off vocabulary: Rising Limb -  Period of time where discharge increases over time Peak/Crest - Maximum Discharge Reached Falling Limb - Period of time where discharge decreases over  time Lag Time - Time between peak rainfall and peak discharge. Baseflow - Flow of water that comes from groundwater seepage. Through Flow - Water that flows through soil to get to stream Storm Runoff - Water that flows on land to the stream Flashy - Rapid rise and fall Subdued - Gradual rise and fall Cumec - Unit of flow equal to one cubic meter of water per second Effects on hydrographs: Urbanization Higher peak, shorter lag time, flashier. children.label: A4 Stream Channel Pattern
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: A4.1 Straight Channel Pattern
children.description: A Straight Channel Pattern is…well…straight. It usually has either a very high or very low slope. They usually have a low sediment load, and have very strong banks usually made of bedrock. However, they are usually very rare in nature, and when they do appear, they are usually very short. They could appear via: fault lines, bedwork gorges, or human-made canals.

children.label: A4.2 Meandering Channel Pattern
children.description: A Meandering Channel looks kinda like a snake, going back and forth. It develops in areas of low slope, and has a fine sediment load, consisting of silt and sand. It has sticky, cohesive banks Composed of clay or rooty soil. They have a steady flow. They form in 5 steps. 1. A straight channel deepens. 2. The river begins to oscillate, undercutting the outer bank, and depositing sediment at the inside of the bend, or point bar. 3. Abrasion deepens the channel, point bars form on the inside of banks. 4. Helicoidal Flow begins creating bends. 5. Erosion progresses forward. You might be curious, what is Helicoidal Flow, also known as the corkscrew motion? It is the spiral-pattern movement of water in meandering river bends. When water enters a meander bend, it piles up on the outside, splashing down due to gravity. Due to pressure, the water moves towards the inside, it resurfaces and, because of centrifugal force, goes back to the outside. To put in simpler terms, it forms when a slightly curvy straight channel pattern, like the one shown above, gradually changes over time when the outside of the bend, or the cut bank, erodes due to faster waters, and the inside of the band, or the point bar, deposits due to slower waters. Some more vocabulary: a meander loop is one of the many u-bends that a meandering channel does. When a meander loop is cut off from the meandering channel, it is called an Oxbow lake. A meander neck is the length of the “hole” in a meander loop. A meander neck cutoff is when the meander neck closes and forms a more efficient route for the water to pass through. This may result in a meander scar, an empty channel, a trace of the dead  meandering channel. Similar to the meander neck cutoff, the meander chute cutoff can happen across a point bar, and usually happens during floods. See image on right.

children.label: A4.3 Braided Channel Pattern
children.description: A Braided Channel look like a normal river, except there are a bunch of islands in the middle of them. appears in moderate to steep slopes, with very high coarse sediment loads, including sand, gravel, and cobbles. They have weak and easily eroded banks, and highly variable discharge due to flashy floods. They form like this: during a flood, a river carries lots of sediment. When the flood ends, the sediment drops, mostly in the middle, forming a small weak island due to deposition, also called Braid Bars.  Because braided channels form in weak areas, they are very unstable. Some niche vocab (NICHE REFERENCE!!!): when a channel cuts across a bar, it is called a Chute. Each individual flowing channel in a braided channel is called a thread. Braided channels are most commonly found in glacial outwash plains, mountain streams with landslide debris, deserts after flash floods, and rivers downstreams of volcanos.  It should also be noted these form quickly, less than a century. The following picture is actually an example for both a braided AND a meandering channel!

children.label: A4.4 Anastomosing Channel
children.description: An Anastomosing Channel 	is very similar to braided in terms of look, but in reality is quite different. For one, its island has life, and are much more stable. The entire thing, in fact, is much more  stable. The channels are all very stable, and there is very little sediment. The sediment is fine, consisting of silt and clay, and rather than a mode rate to steep climate, it develops in a very gentle slope. It has very strong banks, consisting of clay or roots. It moves slow rather than fast, and it usually develops on lowland deltas, swampy plains, and large rivers. Here is how they form: they form in extremely strong banks. Thus, when something blocks the river’s flow, the water rises up and flows over the blockage, forming a new path not necessarily in the same position as the old path. This process of abandoning an original path in favor of a new one is called an anabranch in a process called avulsion. The result is an island in the middle of a stream, but this time much stronger and vegetable-filled. It should be noted these form very slowly; in thousands of years.

children.label: A4.5 Wandering Channel
children.description: A Wandering Channel is a combination of a meandering and braided channels, and actually shown above. An intermediate slope, and a combination of coarse and fine sediment is required, as well as a moderate bank strength. It forms the same way as meandering, but forms bars occasionally. Not much else to add… Now, a vocabulary term you should know is sinuosity, which means how curvy a  stream is. That  is, it is a ratio between the total length of a stream, and the absolute length from the beginning to the end. For example, a river that is perfectly straight would have a sinousity of 1, while a meandering river  might have a sinuosity of 3. Magikal Tabel: River Type Slope(m/m) Velocity Sed. children.label: A5 Sediments
children.description: There are three types of sediment: Bedload, which are coarse particles like sand, gravel, cobbles. These move by rolling, sliding, or bouncing along the bottom, a process called saltation. These usually carry about 5-25% of the total load. Suspended load, which are fine particles like silt, clay, sand. These are carried by the water and kept up by turbulence. The largest particle size a stream can move is called competence, while the finest sediment that is in the suspended load is called the wash load. The total load a stream can carry is called capacity.  These usually carry around 60-90% of the total load. Dissolved load, which are ions like calcium, bicarbonate, and sodium. These are carried with the water, because they are dissolved in them. These come from chemical weathering of rocks, and are in high concentrations in limestone regions, and lower in granite. It is a yellow-ish wild-blown silt, and is very fertile because it is filled with minerals and has good drainage. It forms when wind picks up silt-sized particles from deserts or such and deposits them elsewhere. For example, the Yellow River in china carries a lot of loess. This is also described in F4.3 Soil Formation

children.label: A6 Stream Flow
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: A6.1 Perennial/Intermittent/Ephemeral streams
children.description: Perennial/Significant streams are streams that are present year-round. This is usually due to being connected to groundwater via baseflow (see A6.2). Intermittent streams that are present part of the year. These are usually due to having seasonal discharge inflow stuff, like snow melt or other stuff. Ephemeral streams are streams that are absent unless precipitation exists.

children.label: A6.2 Gaining & Losing Streams
children.description: Gaining streams, or a fluent stream receive water from groundwater surrounding, while losing streams, or an influent stream lose water. What determines this gain/loss is the hydraulic head, or how fast water is moving in a place. Water that has more pressured always goes towards lower pressured waters. This is called baseflow.  Because a stream gains water as it moves downstream, its discharge increases. On the other hand, losing streams will eventually die out because the groundwater steals all its water :O

children.label: A6.3 Calculating the Discharge
children.description: To calculate discharge, you have to know the cross sectional area and the velocity. Usuually, the cross-section of a river is split into 25 to 30 rectangles, like a riemann sum, and the depth and velocity is found for each rectangle. Then, the depth, velocity, and riemann thingy width are multiplied together to get the discharge of a segment. The discharges of all the segments are added together to find the total discharge. Why do we have to do this cat and mouse chase you ask? Well, velocity and depth vary. That’s right! Velocity in rivers are the highest in the center, assuming there are no bends or other willy wonky thingies. In order to find the velocity, a current meter can be used. It has a wheel, that turns when water pushes it, and converts that into a number. Simple. The most common type of current meter is a Price AA Current meter. 6 buckets revolve around a center axis, and the rate of revelusion is turned into velocity. It is also designed to be attached to a wading rod in shallow waters, or mounted above a weight suspended above a cable in deeper waters. It should be noted that in shallow waters, a Pygmy Price Current Meter, a 2/5th version of a price AA, is used instead. There is also the float method: Measure how long a floating object takes to travel a certain distance, and use that to calculate the surface velocity. Then, multiply it by a factor because surface water moves faster than bottom water. This number is roughly 0.9 if the bed is smooth, and roughly 0.8 if the bed is rocky. This is a backup method for using a current meter, though it is less accurate. Now, on to depth. You remember the wading rod from before? It is used to find depth in shallow, calm waters. A person sticks the wading rod, which is like a really long meterstick (METRIC SYSTEM RULES), into the water and reads the label. If the water is too fast or deep, a sounding weight is used instead. It is a weight on a copper wire fishing rod. A person fishes out the fishing rod weight, and reels it lower until they feel impact. They then see how much cable they used, and that is the depth :D. This happens off a boat, of course.

children.label: A7 Stream Pirates
children.description: “Arrr Joe. I’m here to steal all arr monies” “Noooooooooooooooo” A stream pirate is a stream that steals input from another stream. That is to say, stream V, the victim stream, is diverted to feed water into stream P, the evil pirate. (ahoy, scallywags!) Here’s what happens mateys. One river is higher than the other yarr, and erodes better. Thus, the little rascal does some headward erosion with the other river, and when the cliffs finally collapses, since water follows the past of least resistance, the higher stream diverts to the lower stream. A successful pirating! What remains of the former path of the victim stream, is now a beheaded stream. If a tiny trickle of water still flows through the large hollow channel, it is called a misfit stream. One example of this is the 2016 Yukon glacier retreat, caused by global warming causing a glacier to melt.

children.label: A8 Floods
children.description: Floods are caused by sudden and plentiful water, possibly caused by heavy rainfall or prolonged storms, rapid snowmelt. Urbanization, saturated soil, steep terrain, and lack of vegetaion could further worsen flooding. A flood can be described as a N-year flood. This N can be calculated by the following formula: if a stream has Y years of data. Then the Kth largest flood has a reccurence interval, or N, of (Y+1)/K. A recurrence interval of N does not mean a flood would occur once every N years. Rather, it means a flood has a 1/N probability of occurring each year.

children.label: A9 Stream Gauging
children.description: In order to measure the discharge for a stream, a stage sensor is usually used. It’s picture is shown to the right, but essentially what it does is it measures the amount of water pressure above it, which could be translated into a water level. A stage sensor measures the water level roughly every 15 minutes , and converts that into a measure of discharge. The level to discharge curve is then known as the rating curve, usually linear, and the rating curve could be used to calculate discharge from water level in the future. However, a stage sensor used in regular water may be inaccurate, due to all the stupid ripples and waves. Thus, a stilling well is usually used, and the stage sensor is put in there. The water level is the same water level as the one in the stream. An alternate solution would be to use a bubbler level measurement system. Basically, you still a huge metal straw into the water, and blow a gas out, and measure the pressure. Because hydrostatic force stuffs say pressure is (Density of water) * (gravity) * (depth), we can calculate depth quite well. children.label: A10 River Deltas
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: A10.1 Delta Definition & Formation
children.description: A river delta is a depositional landform that forms at a river’s mouth when it flows into a slower body of water, like an ocean, sea, or lake. The sudden drop in water velocity causes sediment to be  dropped, causing salt, silt, and clay to be dropped. This creates  a fan, triangular, or bird’s foot shape. A delta will form if river deposition happens faster than wave, tide, or currents can erode it away. It  forms in 5 steps River erodes sediment and begins transporting it The velocity off the water carrying the sediment plummets as it reaches standing  water It deposits, sorting itself by size before sinking. Sediment buildup creates a bar, a chunk of land that splits  teh channel water into separate  channels This process repeats, leading to progradation where the delta slowly grows seaward over time

children.label: A10.2 Delta Anatomy
children.description: All deltas can be split into three main parts: The upper delta plain is located above the water. Meaning, even at high tide the  upper delta plain stays above water. It can contain freshwater marshes, swamps, and shallow lakes. The lower delta plain sits in the middle and is flooded by tides during high tides. It features slightly salty bays and mangrove swamps. The subaqueous, or underwater, delta lies completely below the water and forms a platform of which the rest of a delta is built. Some more vocabulary: A delta plain is the combination of the upper and lower delta plains. A delta front is the steep, sloping area that faces the open water. The prodelta is the farthest zone where the smallest of the smallest of the particles can settle.

children.label: A10.3 River/wave-dominated Deltas
children.description: A river-dominated delta forms where wave forces are weak. In turn, the shape of the delta is controlled mostly by the river, resulting in a  very outward, irregular outline. One example is the Mississippi river, with a bird’s foot shaped delta shown on the right. A wave-dominated delta forms when  wave forces are strong. Thus,  waves control the delta, creating a classic fan or arc shape. The Nile  River   is an example of this. A tide-dominated delta forms when tidal ranges are long. Strong tidal currents can reshape  the river’s mouth into long narrow funnel-shaped thingys. The Fly River is one example. TODO: Estarine/lacustine deltas?

children.label: A11 Alluvial Fans
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: A11.1 Formation
children.description: Alluvial fans are large cone or fan-shaped piles of sediment such as gravel, sand, or silt that forms when a steep mountain stream suddenly goes into a flat valley floor. When a fast-moving stream rushes down a mountain canyon and hits the wide, flat valley floor, also called the mountain front, their velocity decreases drastically, by around 90%. Meaning, some heavy sediment such as gravel or sand that was previously transported or even eroded are not deposited, depositing huge amounts of sand and gravel. The best place to see alluvial fans is Death Valley, because the mountains are steep, the valley is flat, and there are rare desert thunderstorms. No vegetation or rivers to erode them away as well.

children.label: A11.2 Anatomy
children.description: The apex is the highest point of the fan, located at the mouth of the canyon. This is where the biggest, heaviest sediment that really can’t go that far are deposited. The mid-fan is where medium-sized gravel and sand is deposited. Water flowing through here can form braided streams. The toe (THEORY OF EVERYTHINGGGG) of a fan is where the finest sediments such as silt and clay are deposited. Finally, an incision is when a stream cuts a deep channel in its own fan, meaning instead of the water spreading out and going everywhere it goes through the channel. I should also probably tell you that when multiple alluvial fans collide, it is called a Bajadas. A11.3 Fluvial vs. Dubris-Flow Fan Fan type Process Location Key Feature Fluvial Formed by streamflow Humid/semi-arid mountains Most common. Sediment sorted Debris Flow Formed by a landslide of a mixture of mud, rocks, water. Arid/desert mountains with rare, strong thunderstorms. Sediment unsorted Dangorous

children.label: A11.4 Crevasse Splay
children.description: A crevasse splay is a type of alluvial fan that occurs in the floodplain around a river during a flood stage. When water pressure pushes against the levee, or the raised bank, around it . It finds a weekpoint, or crevasse, and punctures it such that water can flow out and deposit a crevasse splay. The sediment in a crevasse splay can also prevent the water within the crevasse. These spread very fertile soil and water far inland.

children.label: A11 Waterfalls
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: A11.1 Anatomy and Formation
children.description: How are waterfalls formed? When a stream passes through a bank of resistant rock called a caprock, and then a bank of softer rock, the softer rock erodes quicker, creating a height difference in the water above the hard rock and the water above the soft rock. The line where water thus falls is called the fall line, and the point on the stream where  the water falls is called a lip/knickpoint. A plunge pool is formed by the force of the falling water, which carves a basin at the bottom. The water undercuts the soft rock, forming a small hollow cave called  a rock shelter/grotto at the base beneath the hard rock, which eventually collapses, forming a talus/scree.  Then, the cycle repeats again and again as the fall line moves upstream. This  leaves behind a steep-sided, narrow valley called a “gorge.” Because the speed of water increases near a waterfall, the rock near a waterfall can be very smooth due to higher amounts of erosion. This is  not the only way they can form, however. They can also form glacially, when a large glacier erodes a large deeper valley than a small glacier next to it, causing a huge height difference that becomes a waterfall. Yosemite Falls is an example of this Tectonic activity can also create a waterfall, if a “fault scarp, ” a chunk of land uplifted because of tectonic movement, can also create a height difference that translates into a waterfall. A waterfall can also randomly appear, known as a self-formed waterfall. Although people didn’t think this was possible, a study in 2019 found that rivers' randomness could randomly erode a dent in the bed which can slowly become a waterfall. This process can take between 10 to 10,000 years.

children.label: A11.2 Destruction
children.description: Waterfalls “die” when the knickpoint  moves  forward to a point where there is no difference in the hardness of a rock anymore, there is no hard caprock anymore. The slope becomes less steep, and turns into a gentle graded stream, also known as a rapids. Erodability chart: softest -> hardest 1Clay&Silt | 2Sand & Gravel | 3Chalk | 4Shale | 5Siltstone | 6Limestone | 7Tuff | 8Weak Sandstone | 9Strong Sandstone |  10Schist/Phyllite | 11Basalt | 12Granite | 13Quartzite | 14Chert/Flint Usually, rocks of rank 1-6 are  on the bottom and of ranks 9-14 are on the top.

children.label: A11.3 Structure Types of Waterfalls
children.description: Plunge Waterfalls: These  are  waterfalls in which there is an air gap between the water and the cliff. This is because the caprock sticks out like a shelf, and the soft rock underneath gets eroded due to downcutting. One notable example is Angel Falls in Venezuela, the largest uninterrupted plunge waterfall. Horsetail Waterfalls: These are waterfalls in which water descends vertically, but maintains contact with the bedrock all the way down. This is usually because the cliff is slanted or is very rough such that water’s surface tension can keep it pressed up to  the wall. One example is the Bridalveil Falls (Yosemite, USA.) If it is thin enough, it could also be classified as a Bridal Veil Waterfall. Cascade Waterfalls These are waterfalls in which water descends in steps, tumbling instead of falling straight down. This occurs when the hard rock forms in steps. One example would be the Ouzoud Falls in Morocco. Slide Waterfalls These occur when the bedrock forms in a slope such that the water can slide down the slope. These usually occur over a massive unbroken slab of bedrock tilted at a moderate angle. They are often polished by past glacial activity. One example is the Gullfoss in Iceland. Block/Sheet/Cataract Waterfalls These are basically plunge waterfalls, except the river is very wide. Thus, it creates a huge sheet of water. There are no rocks in  the middle to split its flow as well. Some of the Niagra Falls is a sheet waterfall. Segmented Waterfall: These occur when water is split into separate, individual streams as it falls, due to rock  walls, islands or boulders between them. This is because differential erosion can create rock pillars that can isolate streams. One example is Iguazu Falls (Argentina/Brazil), with 275 separate segments! Tiered Waterfall: These are basically cascades,  but much thicker. It allows the water to flow a little between dropping it again. One example would be Yosemite Falls (USA). Punchbowl Waterfall: This occurs when water  descends in a very narrow flow, and then spreads out in a wide, circle pool at the bottom. This is because the narrow flow holds a lot of energy in it, and it eventually erodes a huge plunge pool into the ground. One famous example of this is Punch Bowl Falls. Fan Waterfall: This occurs when water spreads out horizontally as it descends, becoming wider and wider. This is because while the rock at the top is narrow, it flares outward. Water thus naturally spreads sideways to  fill the expanding space. One example of this is  Vøringsfossen.

children.label: A12 Stream Evolution
children.description: Your youthful stream pokemon is evolving! *flashy flashy* Congratulations! Your youthful stream pokemon evolved into a mature stream pokemon! A youthful stream is like a child. It is very energetic, and its main goal is to cut downwards towards the base level. They are usually straight. A mature stream had  already cut  down to sea level, and thus focuses on downcutting the surrounding  rocks. It also begins to meander around.  An old-age stream is in its final stage. It is very low energy, and typically has extreme meanders. More info on the table below: Feature Youthful Stream Mature Stream Old Age Stream Slope Steep Moderate Low, flat Valley Shape Narrow, V-shaped Wider Broad, flat floodplain Channel Pattern Straight/Irregular Meandering Extreme Meandering Dominant Process Downward Erosion Sideways Erosion Deposition Energy & Flow High Moderate Low A13. Laminar vs. Turbulent Flow At the time I’m writing this, this is A13, and I am not planning to write A14. How much money are you betting that I write all the way to A15? Laminar flow is a peaceful flow. It looks smooth, glassy, the  water moves  in straight parallel sheets. Its energy use is very efficient - it uses very little energy to push water forward. Turbulent flow, on the other  hand, is rough, choppy, eddies everywhere,  they move in random swirls and currents. They are inefficient, they waste energy on swirls and noise. However, Turbulent flow is faster than Laminar flow. Why? You cannot make water go fast without having it splash and going everywhere. Also the splashes make it so that Turbulent flow is thoroughly mixed while Laminar flow’s sheets, also known as Streamlines, allow zero mixing between layers. Turbulent flow is much more widespread, in almost ALL rivers and streams! Meanwhile, Laminar Flow is found in groundwater seeping through soil or thin films of water on rocks. Turbulent flow can also create potholes, bowl-shaped, or cylindrical hollows made into the bed of a river.  They form when sediment fast-moving  water carries into a joint or fracture in bedrock. The continuous grinding of the sediment in this crack deepens and widens it. As it grows it can merge with other potholes, creating complex, connected spaces. The Reynold’s Number determines if a flow is Laminar or Turbulent. It is the velocity*depth/viscosity (the viscosity of water is about 10^(-6)). If the Reynold’s number is <500, it is Laminar. If fit is >2000, it is turbulent. No one talks about the middle, ok?

children.label: A14.1 Morphology
children.description: Channel - Depression river flows through Bank - Sides of channel Bed - Bottom of Channel Floodplain - Land next to river that gets covered with water during flood Levee - Raised land surrounding river to prevent flooding in floodplain Terrace - Abandoned floodplain after channel eroded downwards. Watershed/Drainage Basin - Area of land where all precipitation drains. Divide - Division between two watersheds

children.label: A14.2 Hydrology
children.description: Discharge - Volume of water flowing past a point per second Velocity - Speed of water Turbulent - Chaotic water flow caused by interferences like rocks or boulders. Laminar Flow - Smooth water flow Baseflow - Normal flow of a river supplied by groundwater Stormflow / Bankfull - High flow during a storm

children.label: A14.3 Erosion, Transport, Deposition
children.description: Scour - Erosion caused by fast water Erosion - Wearing away of banks and bed Downcutting - Erosion that cuts vertically Lateral Erosion - Erosion that cuts sideways Headward Erosion - Erosion that extends the dip in the channel uphill Suspended load - particles that float in th water Bed Load - Particles that bounce on the bed in the water Saltation - The bouncing motion of the bed load Traction - When large boulders are rolled or pushed Deposition - When sediment is dropped Channel Degradation - When a river degrades its bed over time due to erosion Channel Aggradation - When a river shallows over time due to deposition.

children.label: A14.4 River’s Length
children.description: Headwaters/Source Zone - Fast, high, steep, erosion dominates. Transfer Zone/Mid-Reach - Medium flow and slope. Wider, transport dominates. Depositional Zone/Lower Reach - Low flow and slope, warm water, deposition dominates.

children.label: A14.5 Rill Features
children.description: Rill - Very tiny, shallow drainage channel cut into soil. Gully - Large, deeper erosion channel, still small, but not that small Runoff - Rainwater that flows over land surface instead of becoming groundwater Interfluve - Higher ridge of land between two rills or streams

children.label: A14.6 Larger Features
children.description: Tributary - River that feeds into another river. Distributary - River that is fed by another river Meander - Large curve in river Oxbow Lake - When a meander is cut off, forming a lake Yazoo Stream - Smaller tributary running parallel to a large river that can’t enter Delta - Fan-shaped deposit at mouth of river Alluvial Fan - Delta that occurs when mountain stream hits valley floor Plunge Pool - Deep hole at based of waterfall Reach - Uniform section of river. Thalweg - line connecting deepest points along river channel Wetted Perimeter - Total length of riverbank and bed touching the water

children.label: B1 Formation
children.description: Groundwater appears when rain or snowmelt seeps into the waterin a process called recharge. Gravity pulls the water down until it comcletely fills an area, forming an underground reseviour called an aquifer.

children.label: B2 Parts of groundwater
children.description: The groundwater can be split into two parts: the zone of aeration and the zone of saturation. The zone of aeration is the dry soil. In zone of aeration, there are several subzones: The soil water zone is where plants’ roots and organisms dwell. Water sticks onto the tiny pores on the top soil in this region. The intermediate zone is where water trickles downwards as a result of gravity, because the composition of the soil around it has less pores. Capillary Fringe is where capillary action, basically when water travels against the force of gravity up due to capillary actions happens because of the compact soil which acts like thin straws. The zone of saturation, on the other hand, is the area where groundwater actually exists. It has no air, and has water filling every single hole in there. It is also dynamic in this planet. Meaning, it moves over time, going from placing from high pressure to regions of low pressure. Because, say it with me kids, water moves from regions of high pressure to regions of low pressure.

children.label: B3 Types of Aquifers
children.description: POV: Corporate wants you to find the difference between an unconfined, confined, and perched aquifer. An unconfined aquifer is like a bucket. It is just like a blob of heavily saturated soil, with no hard rock layer above it. It is open. This has the negative side effect of, say I pour acid on the surface, it will make its way down to the aquafir.On the other hand, confined aquifers have like hard clay-filled rock layer on the top and bottom the aquifer, which means water has to travel a long time in order to get to the aquifer. This hard rock layer has the upside of blocking pollutants. A perched aquifer, the final one, is similiar to an unconfined aquifer. However, instead of lying below the water table, it lies above the water table on a small sheet of unpermeable material. An Aquitard, which rhymes with something unfortunate, is an aquifer that hogs all the water it recieves. An aquiclude is very lonely. It deosn’t collect nor release water. It just stays there.

children.label: B4 Wells
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: B4.1 Well Types
children.description: You know what wells are. There are two types of wells: A water table well is a well into an unconfined aquifer, and requires manual pumping. On the other hand, an artesian well is a well into a confined aquifer with clay rock on both sides. Since the pressure in there is large, the water will shoot up to a point. In fact, a floating artesian well is when this point is higher than the ending point of the well.

children.label: B4.2 Cone of Depression
children.description: When water is quickly sucked up through the well pipe, a low-pressure zone is created, and water surrounding rushes in to fill it. When water is sucked out faster than dirt can replace it, it causes a “cone of depression”, with a “radius of influence.” Why this matters, I may never know. It lowers the water level though.

children.label: B5 Saltwater Intrusion
children.description: A saltwater intrusion happens when a freshwater aquifers turns….salty 🧂🧂🧂🧂🧂 It could be created when people overpump an aquifer, or extended droughts, causing a lack of freshwater in the aquifer, of which saltwater takes its place. Either way, it makes aquifer water unable to drink or use to irrigate crops. How can this be fixed you ask? There are freeeee methods: Artificial Recharge Wells are probably the most common. You inject freshwater at a certain spot, and it is best if it is between the saltwater aquifer and the ocean, and it is also optimal if the sediment in the injected spot is corase so the water can travel down fast and build pressure. This pressure pushes the salt water out 😀 We’re building a (clay) wall. A big beautiful wall. To block the evil saltwater immigrants from coming into out pure, awesome, freshwater aquifer. ADR. Amazing, daring, rapters. Send them in to absorb all the salt!!! Jk uhhh abstraction, desalination, recharge. Take the saltwater out, osmosis the water out, and then put the freshwater back.

children.label: B6 Groundwater Discharge
children.description: Groundwater moves. I like to move it mov- Here are some stupid formulas I ripped off gemini. I hope no one sues me! Discharge: Q = K * i * A. K is hydraulic conductivity, or how easily fluids passes through stuff, i is the slope of the water table, and A is the cross-sectional area. Velocity: V = K * I / N.  N is the object’s porosity Hydraulic conductivity chart: Gravel Coarse Sand Silt Clay 0.01-0.1 0.0001-0.001 0.000001-0.00001 0.000000000001-0.000000001

children.label: B7 Porosity
children.description: Now about porosity…it is the total volume of the void space in something divided by the total space, void and sediments. A primary porosity are pores that were there since the formation of sediment, but secondary porosity are pores that were eventually created. Finally, what I described in the first sentence was total porosity, but effective porosity, in which void space is any space water can reach, is more useful. Related to porosity we have specific yield and retention. Specific yield is the amount of water that can be drained out via the natrual forces of gravity

nodes.label: C River Valleys
nodes.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: C1 Formation
children.description: A river valley starts its life as a normal stream. A stream’s transformation into a river valley has  two parts: downcutting and  widening, or erosion and weathering. During downcutting, rain or melted snow collect sediment like sand or gravel into the river, which scratches the riverbed. This process is called abrasion. This lets the force of the water to break it. This creates a very narrow, steep-sided channel, that has a cross-section that looks like the letter “V.” Once it had reach the maximum erosion level, usually sea level, it then begins widening . The river swings from side to side, as it is a meandering river. This force could undercut, or erode away, the bottom of a bank, which could eventually collapse and tumble. Over  time, this slowly makes the ways less steep, and widens the river valley.

children.label: C2 River Valley Locations
children.description: Mountain Headwater Valley - These originate at the top of the mountains…usually near the river’s source, in the mountain ranges. They usually have a steep gradient (see C3) between 100-500+ ft/mi, and are narrow and V-shaped. These have very little floodplain, and have fast, turbulent flow, and are usually made of rough material. They   are usually straight/braided channel patterns, and appear in the Rocky Mountains, Appalachian, and Sierra Nevadas. Piedmont valleys - The piedmont is the zone between the mountains and the lowlands. These originate at the base of the mountains, where the slope slowly declines. These have moderate gradients between 10-100 ft/mi, and a more significant floodplain. They have gravel, sand, and silt from the mountains. These are usually wandering channel patterns, and some examples are the Colorado, Atlantic coast, and California’s Central Valley piedmonts. Lowland Valley - These originate in  the lowlands…which are…low lands….wow…facinating…gee. They have a gentle gradient between 1-10 ft/mi, and a wide, flat floodplain. It has fine sediment; sand, silt, and clay. The channel pattern is usually meandering. Some examples would be  the Upper Mississippi, Ohio River, and Red River of North  Valleys. Coastal Plain Valley - These occur near the ocean. It  has an extremely gentle gradient less than 1ft/mi, nearly flat. It has an extremely wide floodplain, and very  slow flow. It has swampy, marshy conditions due to poor drainage, and fine sediment of silt and clay. These are usually meandering or anastomosing channel patterns.

children.label: C3 Gradients
children.description: A gradient is the slope of a river valley. It is the change in elevation divided by the horizontal distance. The gradient of a river could tell stuff about a river type. These are usually measured in ft/mi or m/km. It should be noted that a higher gradient usually means a river is moving faster, because a faster river means more downcutting erosion, which means a higher erosion. Interestingly, streams near the headwaters, or the source, will have a higher gradient. This is because the flow would be faster, which meant there will be more vertical erosion, creating a  steeper gradient. Meanwhile, in the mouth there is a slower flower, which means there is more deposition instead.

children.label: C4 Clasts
children.description: A clast is an individual piece of rock or mineral, and it is a building block of a detrital sedimentary rocks. A detrital sedimentary rock being a rock formed by broken or weathered of pre-existing rocks. SIZE: This is the size scale, also known as the Udden-Wentworth Scale, is shown below. Unit: mm Clay Silt Sand Granule Pebble Cobble Boulder <0.002 0.002-0.062 0.062-2 2-4 4-64 64-256 >256 Shale/ Mudstone Shale Sandstone Conglomerate/Berccia Conglomerate/Berccia Most common rock found ROUNDING: Angular - Sharp Angles Sub-rounded - All the angles were smoothed off Rounded - No corners left The farther a rock is transported the rounder it gets. COMPOSITION: Quartz - This is the most common because it is hard and chemically stable Feld-spar - This is also common, but it weathers faster than quartz Lithic Fragments - Pieces of existing rocks Mica - Flat, platy, shiny clasts Heavy Minerals - Dense clasts like zircon, garnet, or magnetite.

children.label: C5 The Base Level
children.description: The base level is the lowest elevation a river can erode. There are two types of base levels: there is the ultimate base level, which is like the absolute limit, and a local base level, which is ab obstacle specific to a location that prevents erosion. The base level can determine the gradient of a river from its source to its end. During places  high above the base level, there would be a steep slope, fast water, and high erosion power. This is because the water has a higher gravitational potential energy, and thus moves faster, which means  it  erodes more, which increase  the gradient. It is the opposite for places where the water is low above the base level.

children.label: C6 Rejuvenated Valleys
children.description: Rejuvenated Valleys are when a river valley is given a new life - that is, the river’s erosive powers regenerate, and the valley, which became dormant, becomes vibrant again and downcuts again. This can be because of a variety of reasons: Tectonic uplift can increase river gradient, speeding up the river The base level could drop, like during the ice ages, and the river cuts deeper to reach it Climate Change could increase rainfall, increasing discharge. Land could rise after glacier melt, increasing the river slope. A pirate stream(see A7), can capture another stream, increasing discharge. A rejuvenated valley tends to be: V-shaped, with deep meanders. It tends to be steep, its sediments coarse, and its floodplain narrow or absent. Entrenched Meanders are meanders that have cut downward into the land, creating meandering canyons. A River Terrace are the abandoned floodplain that the valley, before rejuvenating, used as their floodplain. They look like “steps” on valley walls.
