nodes.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: D1 Salts
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: D1.1 Types of Salts
children.description: Ions found in lakes are typically the same as the ions in rivers and groundwaters…because rivers  flow into lakes… Cations: Calcium (Ca²⁺), Magnesium (Mg²⁺), Sodium (Na⁺), Potassium (K⁺) Anions: Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), Carbonate (CO₃²⁻), Sulfate (SO₄²⁻), Chloride (Cl⁻), Nitrate (NO₃⁻), orthophosphate (PO₄³⁻) The ionic ratios of these salts determine the chemical facies, which can find the type of lakes.

children.label: D1.2 Salt Origin
children.description: Salts originate in mainly four ways: Rock Weathering: Rainwater grabs CO2 from the air and soil, which makes it  slightly acidic. It  then  thus dissolves: Limestone, which dissolves easily, releasing Calcium (Ca²⁺),  Magnesium (Mg²⁺), and Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) Igneous rocks, like granite or obsidian, are stronger, but over time release Sodium (Na⁺), Potassium (K⁺), silica (SiO₂), and orthophosphate (PO₄³⁻) Ancient marine sediments are old seabeds compressed into rock, which easily dissolves into leftover salt (NaCl) and gypsum (CaSO₄). Atmospheric Deposition When  ocean  waves break,  tiny droplets  of seawater are whipped into  the air. These extremely tiny droplets  are carried by winds hundreds off miles inland, where they slowly fall into  the lake.  They deliver cyclic salts,  mainly NaCl. Cyclic salts meaning they are recycled from the ocean. When wind picks up particles from deserts or dry lakebeds, or playas, which slowly fall into the lake, carbonates like calcite or sulfates like gypsum can be deposited. Subsurface  stuffs Groundwater contributes a majority of a lake’s salt load. Groundwater, because it moves really slowly, has a lot of time to dissolve salts. In dry regions, it often passes through buried salt deposits left by prehistoric seas. Flippin’ underwater plumes can also have an effect, as these can provide Silica, Li, B, As, sulfate (SO₄²⁻) and are key in volcanic crater lakes. Human Impact Burning fossil fuels can also oxidize fuel-bound sulfur and nitrogen. In the form of acid rain, Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) and Nitrate (NO₃⁻). Industrial Processes such as smelting, cement production, and chemical manufacturing can result in Chloride (Cl⁻), Calcium (Ca²⁺) from cement dust, and trace amounts of As, Se, and Hg. Agriculture stuffs such as Fertilizers and animal waste decomposition can create  ammonia, which nitrifies into Nitrate (NO₃⁻) in water. Biomass Burning  can result in Potassium (K⁺) and Nitrate (NO₃⁻) Road dust & construction - Concrete, asphalt, and tires  gonna get broken,  resulting in Calcium (Ca²⁺),  Magnesium (Mg²⁺), Carbonate (CO₃²⁻), and Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)

children.label: D1.3 Classifying Lakes by Salinity
children.description: Lakes have  5 classes of salinity. These  5 classes can also have an impact on the sediment type off the lake. Salinity class Salt % (g/L) (Hammer 1986) Sediment Fresh <0.5 Detrital clays, silts sand. Marl (CaCO₃), iron, manganese oxides Subsaline 0.5-3 Clastic sediments, Some calcite (CaCO₃) and Marl (CaCO₃) Hyposaline 3-20 Calcite (CaCO₃), with some argonite and high-Mg calcite Mesosaline 20-50 Gypsum crystals (prismatic, lenticular, twinned desert rose.) Calcite. Hypersaline >50 Halite (NaCl), gypsum. Really salty-> thenardite (Na₂SO₄), mirabilite (Na₂SO₄·10H₂O), trona (Na₃H(CO₃)₂·2H₂O), sylvite (KCl), carnallite (KMgCl₃·6H₂O).

children.label: D1.4 Phosphates(PO₄³⁻) and Nitrates(NO₃⁻)
children.description: Although phosphates and nitrates may play a similar role, they originate differently. Phosphates in lakes mostly originate from the chemical weathering of apatite, or calcium phosphate. Nitrates, however, emerge usually from  the nitrogen cycle that I won’t bore you with. Interestingly, phosphates are usually the limiting factor in freshwater lakes, while nitrates in marine/estuarine systems. They  primarily act  as a fertilizer for lakes, and trigger eutrophication,  where  over-nutrition leads to algae explosion, which can degrade water quality. This  causes hypoxia/anoxia because the algae sucks out all the oxygen. Also because  of this, pH is raised  during  the  day during photosynthesis, and dropped at night.. These  swings can stress aquatic   life. Algae  can also block  sunlight, shading out underwater plants. When the bottom water runs out of the oxygen, the phosphorus trapped in the mud is released back into the water  because the iron  the phosphorus is bound to changes form into a reduced  state. This forms a positive feedback loop, which can be broken with Aluminum  Sulfate or Lanthanum Clay,  which binds to the phosphate at the bottom. Depending on the amount of phosphate and nitrate, a  lake may be classified in different ways: Trophic State Phosphorous (µg/L) Nitrogen (µg/L) Info Oligotrophic <10 <400 Cold-water fish. Plants are sparse, deep. Mesotrophhic 10-20 400-600 Warm-water do better than cold-water. Good mix of underwater plants. Eutrophic >20 >600 No coldwater fish. Floating plants takeover. Hypereutrophic >100 >1500 No plants.  Toughest  species survive. Note: µg/L is  one millionth of a gram.

children.label: D1.5 Open and Closed Lakes
children.description: A closed/endorheic/terminal lake has no outlet to the ocean, a river, or another body of. In short, it is independent, and water can only leave through evaporation. As a result, salinity increases over time, and these lakes often become saline or hypersaline. It can, however, have a river flowing into it or groundwater going into it. Meaning, there are no rivers taking water and salts out of the lake. Some examples are: Caspian, Aral, Salton, and Dead Seas, the Great  Salt Lake, and Lake Titicaca. An open/exorheic lake has an outlet to an ocean or another lake. Thus, the salinity stays low, in fresh or subsaline, and water  levels are more stable. Some examples: Lake Superior -> St Mary’s River -> Lake Huron -> -> -> Atlantic Ocean Lake Victoria ->  White  nile ->  Mediterranean Sea Lake Baikal -> Angara River  -> Yenisei River -> Arctic Ocean Great Lakes -> St. Lawrence River -> Atlantic Ocean Lake Tanganyika -> Lukuga River -> Congo River  -> Atlantic Ocean Lake Michigan-Huron -> St. Clair  River -> Lake Erie -> N. Falls -> Lake Ontario -> Atlantic

children.label: D2 Thermal Stratification and Mixing
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: D2.1 Lake Layers
children.description: During the summer, a lake splits  into 3  layers that do not  mix. The topmost layer is called the Epilimnion. This is  the warm,  sunny surface water at the top. The middle layer is called the Metalimnion is the sharp decrease in temperature, known as the thermocline. The lowest layer is called the Hypolimnion, is the cold, dark, and dense water at the bottom. You can find more info at D5.1 Lake Regions.

children.label: D2.2 Thermal Mixing Patterns
children.description: There are many types of lakes that mix in different durations…yeah let’s just begin. Dimictic Lakes mix two times a year. During the summer, a hot Epilimnion is formed on the surface while a cold Hypolimnion is formed at the bottom. During the fall, as autumn air cools the surface water, it becomes denser and sinks. This eventually destroys the thermal cline, and winds easily mix the lake from top to bottom. During the winter, water freezes and an ice layer floats on the top. Below, a cold layer of water below 4 degrees celsius floats above the warmer water below. During the spring, the ice thaws and the  lake  is now uniform in temperature. Winds thus easily push the  entire water column, and the lake mixes completely from  top to bottom. Polymictic Lakes mix very often. They are shallow lakes, typically less than  15-20 feet deep, located in temperate or tropical environments. Cold polymictic lakes appear in very cold  areas, in which frozen, shallow lakes thaw during the summer and mix really easily with the wind.  Warm polymictic lakes appear in tropical or warm regions, where the sun heats  the entire shallow water column evenly every day, and night  cooling makes the surface cooler and thus denser, and thus turning over the lake. Amictic Lakes never mix. These are permanently ice-covered  lakes, found in places like Antarctica or the Arctic. Meromictic Lakes never fully mix. They are chemically stratified, usually because the deep water is much saltier, therefore denser,  than the surface water.  They can form in arid climates where evaporation concentrates salts, or deep sinkholes or volcanic craters where salty groundwater  seeps in at the bottom. Monomictic  Lakes mix one time a year. There are cold and warm monomictic lakes. Warm monotonic lakes  occur in warm climates, in which  the thermocline is very thin such that during the winter, the coldness is just enough such that it can mix.  Cold ones are the opposite.

children.label: D2.3 Thermal Mixing Pattern Locations
children.description: Mixing Type Latitude Typical  Regional Examples Amictic > 66 N/S Antarctica, High Arctic Meromictic Any latitude Great Salt Lake, Dead Sea Cold Polymictic 50-66 N/S Siberia, Scandinavia, Alpine Rockies Warm  Polymictic 0-30 N/S Florida, the  Amazon, Texas prairie ponds Cold Monomictic 45-60 N/S Pacific Northwest  in USA, New Zealand Warm Monomictic 20-45  N/S Equatorial Africa, Mediterranean lakes Dimictic 30-55 N/S US  great lakes, Switzerland, Germany

children.label: D3 Lake  Formation
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: D3.1 Glacial  Lakes
children.description: Glacial lakes form when glaciers scrape material as they move, leaving holes that fill with water. Subtype Formation Example Kettle  Lake A block of ice breaks off from a glacier and gets buried in sediment. After it melts and the  dirt above falls, it leaves a shallow circular lake. Walden Pond  (MA, USA) Many Minnesota lakes. Cirque Lake/Tarn A glacier  carves  out a bowl-shaped depression, called a cirque, at the  head of a mountain valley. When  the ice melts,  water fills the bowl. Lake  Geneva (Switzerland) Flathead  Lake (MT,  USA) Moraine Dammed  Lake A glacier pushes  a pile  of debris, or moraine, in front of it. When  the glacier retreats,  the moraine acts as a dam, trapping water. Lake Geneva (Switzerland) Flathead  Lake (MT, USA) Glacial Valley Lake/Finger Lake A glacier makes  a river valley  wider and deeper. When the ice  melts, the valley fills with water. The Finger Lakes (NY,  USA) Lake Windermere (UK) Paternoster Lake As a glacier moves down a mountain and alternates sections of hard and soft bedrock, eroding a “stair-step pattern.” Water collects, dammed by moraines. Rocky Mountains, Alps

children.label: D3.2 Tectonic Lakes
children.description: Tectonic  lakes  occur  when  the movements of  plate tectonics create depressions that fill with water. Subtype Formation Example Rift Valley Lake Continental plates pull apart, creating a huge, deep valley, also called a rift, that fills with water. Lake Baikal (Russia) Deepest lake in the world Lake  Tanganyika (Africa) Graben Lake A graben lake is  a type of rift valley  lake in which the lake is located on the flat ground  at the bottom  of the  rift valley, trapping  a graben lake between  two  horsts. Lake Baikal (Russia) Lake Tahoe (CA/NV, USA) Lake  Tanganyika (Africa) Faultscarp Lake When two tectonic plates  want  to slide next  to each other, but can’t, because friction,  and then the  stress overcomes  the friction, the rocks can suddenly slip  past each other. If the slip is vertical, then the ground surface directly above the fault, along with half your house, moves with it.  A  fault scarp thus appears, a huge cliff that appeared out of nowhere. This can block rivers, and act as huge dams, creating lakes. Pyramid Lake (NV, USA)

children.label: D3.3 Volcanic Lakes
children.description: Volcanic lakes  form  when  volcanic activity creates depressions that  fill with  water. Subtype Formation Example Crater Lake A volcano erupts and collapses inward, forming a depression called a caldera, which fills with water. Crater Lake  (OR, USA) Lake Toba  (Indonesia) Volcanic-Dammed Lake Lava flows  from  a volcano block   a river valley, creating a dam that traps water and creates a lake. Cascade  Range  (USA) Maar Lake A volcanic explosion blasts a crater into the ground when magma meets groundwater. The crater fills with water. Germany, Alaska, New Zealand Lava-Tube  Lake When  a lava tube, or an underground  tunnel formed by flowing  lava, collapses, a long depression is formed tat fills with water. Rare. Some in Hawaii, Iceland, and  the Galapagos Islands

children.label: D3.4 Fluvial/River Lakes
children.description: Fluvial lakes form  when river processes create depressions  that  fill with water. Subtype Formation Example Oxbow Lake Plunge Pool Lake Alluvial Fan Lake Delta lake

children.label: D3.5 Karst Lakes
children.description: Karst lakes form when water dissolves soluble bedrock, like limestone or gypsum, creating depressions that fill with water. Subtype Formation Example Sinkhole Lake A cave roof collapse due to  the dissolution of the  limestone underneath, forming a  sinkhole.  Water  fills tihs  depression Many in FL, USA Yucatan Peninsula (Mexico) Karst Valley  Lake A  large flat-floored depression in  a karst landscape that forms overtime.  It seasonally fills  with  water during wet  periods. Croatia, Slovenia Dinaric  Alps

children.label: D3.6 Landslide/Debris-Dammed Lakes
children.description: Landslide  lakes form  when  a landslide, rockslide, or a debris flow dams (D-A-M) a river valley, that creates  a lake behind it. Subtype Formation Example Landslide-Dammed Lake Rock and soil slides down a slope, damming a river, forming a lake behind it. Lake Sarez (Tajikistan) Quake Lake (MT, USA) Rock Avalanche Lake An  avalanche,  or a sturzstrom, dams a  river, forming a lake beind it.  This is a more extreme version of a  Landslide-Dammed  lake. Canadian Rockies, Swiss Alps

children.label: D3.7 Coastal Lakes
children.description: Coastal  Lakes are formed when coastal processes trap water behind barriers. Subtype Formation Example Lagoon Long  Shore Drift  creates a  sandbar and traps  a bay of  water, forming a lagoon. Partial connection to ocean. Venetian Lagoon (Italy) Chilika Lake (India) Pamlico Sound (NC, USA) Coastal  Dune Lake A  stream gets dammed by sand dunes, and accumulates into a lake. When a C.D. lake is full, it actually  flows out to connect  with the ocean. Tea-colored. Oregon, Florida, New Zealand, etc. Isolated Marine Basin Lake Cut off part of the ocean.  Zero connection  to ocean. Caspian Sea Aral Sea

children.label: D3.8 Anthropogenic/Man-made Lakes
children.description: These lakes are created by human activity. Subtype Formation Example Reservoir A  dam is built across a river, creating  an artificial lake that can be used. Lake Mead (NV/AZ, USA) Lake Powell (UT/AZ, USA) Quarry/Mine Pit  Lake Abandoned mines fill with water. This  water is often acidic due to exposed minerals. Berkeley Pit (MT, USA) UK, Germany Farm Pond Small, artificial ponds used for agricultural use. IDK Ornamental Lake Artificial  lakes built for recreation Central Park Lake (NY, USA)

children.label: D3.9 Eolian/Aeolian/Wind Lakes
children.description: Eolian lakes form  when wind erosion creates depressions  that fill with  water, often seasonally. Subtype Formation Example Deflation Basin Lake Wind blows away loose sediment, creating a shallow depression. This depression may fill with water. Many in  the High Plains  (USA),  Sahel region (Africa), Central Asia Oasis A depression in a desert reaches the water table, creating a permanent lake or wetland that supports vegetation and wildlife. Many in the Sahara Desert, Arabian Desert, and Mojave Desert (USA) Playa Lake A shallow, temporary lake in an arid region that fills after rainfall and dries up quickly, leaving a flat, salty lakebed called a playa. Great Salt Lake Desert (UT, USA), Death Valley (CA, USA), Lake Eyre (Australia) *dying noises*  god  forgive  me *coff koff* i copied most of this table from deepseek

children.label: D3.10 Organic Lakes
children.description: These occur when  living organisms create a lake. Subtype Formation Example Peat-Dammed Lake Peat, decomposed plant matter, blocks drainage in a wetland,  creating a lake. Often acidic and low in nutrients. Common in Ireland, Siberia, and Canada. Beaver-Dammed Lake Beaver build dam. Dam make lake. North America and Eurasia. Coral Lake Coral   reefs trap water. Make  lake. Some in coral atoll lagoons. *dying noises*  we dun *cofff*

children.label: D3.11 Types of Lake  Trivia
children.description: The most circular lake is a crater  lake.  The most irregular would be a glacial valley lake/finger lake. Rift valley lakes are typically the deepest and oldest  lakes, while glacial lakes in general are the most common type of lake,  along with the youngest. and the freshest. Note  that Kettle and Cirque lakes are  the most fresh of these.  The   saltiest type of lake is an Isolated Marine Basin Lake, though Playa Lakes are also very salty. Impact crater lakes are extremely clear, and are also the rarest  type of lake. The most nutrient-rich lake is Oxbow Lake, while the most nutrient-poor lake is Cirque Lake. The most toxic lake would be a Mine Pit Lake. The  most temporary lake is a Playa Lake. Finally, the highest lake  is a Cirque Lake, while the lowest lake is a Rift Valley Lake.

children.label: D4 Lake Destruction
children.description: No content found under this heading yet.

children.label: D4.1 Natural Death
children.description: This is the most common natural death. This occurs when, over thousands of years, a lake slowly turns into a wetland, and then slowly into dryland. When a lake gradually accumulates nutrients, phosphates and nitrates (See D1.4), which causes more plant/algae growth. These sink to the bottom after they die, and decompose, which consumes the dissolved oxygen and creates sediment called much. As the lake becomes shallower and shallower, it eventually becomes a marsh, then a swamp, then a forest. The lake dies a natural, peaceful death. D4.2 Geological Death. A.K.A. got hit by a car This would be an "unnatural death,” like getting hit by a car.  There are three main ways: Climatic Drying. If  a region dries for a long period of  time, the lake’s water can  evaporate faster than its source can regenerate is. As such, the lake shrinks and withers away. Tectonics and glacial shifts. Earthquakes shift the ground, cracking the lake’s basin, allowing water to drain out. Or, a glacial moraine dam erupts, causing a lake to rapidly drain. Chemical death. This may be like a coma.. While not technically dead, a lake can beomce so acidic or salty that most life cannot survive.

children.label: D4.3 Human-Induced Death
children.description: Human activities dump massive amounts of phosphate and nitrate into the water. As such, algae blooms, decomposition sucks oxygen out, and fish suffocate and die. Deforestation, construction, or poor farming practices can cause massive soil erosion, filling a lake in, covering the floor and killing any plants or breeding grounds in there. Humans build dams, divert rivers for irrigation, or extract massive amounts of groundwater. When the water flowing into a lake is cut off, the lake evaporates and shrivels up. Chemical/Thermal Pollution: Industrial dumping of heavy metals and toxins can poison the exosystem, dying fish.

children.label: D5 Lake Regions

children.label: D5.1 Thermal  Stratification Zones
children.description: [COPIED FROM D2.1] During the summer, a lake splits  into 3  layers that do not  mix. The topmost layer is called the Epilimnion. This is  the warm,  sunny surface water that is  usually  18-26 celsius. It  is  heated by the  sun and wind, and because warm water is less dense, it floats on top of the denser cold water of the bottom layers. The middle layer is called the Metalimnion, also known  as the thermocline. This is the layer in which there is a rapid or sharp decrease in  temperature, often by 7-8  celsius per meter. This thermocline is the reason  why the topmost layer can mix with the bottom ones The bottommost layer is called the Hypolimnion, is the cold, dark, and dense water at  the bottom, hovering at around  3-5 celsius. It is an oxygen-deprived “dead zone” because it receives no oxygen from the surface due to the thermal stratification, and whatever oxygen WAS down  there was used up by the decomposing organic matter.

children.label: D5.2 Lentic Zonation
children.description: DISCLAIMER: This only applies to a Lentic Ecosystems(still, freshwater lake) Lentic Zonation  is mostly based on light zones. Kinda. The Littoral Zone is located in the shoreline,  or near the shore. It is the shallow, sunlit water next to the short. It ends when rooted plants can’t grow anymore. Because lots of sunlight hits this place, the temperature in this region fluctuates  the most. The bottom, known as the benthos. This is the most biodiverse zone as well. Organisms living here include: Rooted aquatic plants such as cattails, reeds, or water lilies can exist here; insects such as mosquito larvae, dragonfly nymphs; crustaceans like crayfish; amphibians like frogs and salamanders; snails; and small fish like perch and minnows. Birds like herons also feed here. The Limnetic Zone is in the top layer of the open water, in the sunlit surface.  It is sunny, and although sunlight does penetrate here, it does not reach the bottom because it is too deep. Thus,  it is warmer near the surface and cooler at the bottom, and  the benthos is out of reach. This place has a lot of floating life. Organisms living here include: phytoplankton, zooplankton such as copepods and daphnia, and larger predatory fish such as bass and trout. The Profundal Zone is below the limnetic zone, light never reaches here. It is very  cold and  stable year-round, usually around 4 degrees celsius. Life  here are heterotrophs, meaning they must consume food or decaying matter. Organisms include: lake trout, whitefish, crayfish, and organisms that feed on “marine snow”. The Benthic Zone is at the very bottom  of the lake. This zone overlaps with the others, and can range from being lit, under littoral, or dark, under profundal. Decomposers and detritivores thrive here. Organisms such  as  worms, insect larvae, bacteria, fungi, and claims live here.

It has the highest dissolved oxygen ,and the coolest water. There, organisms of low tolerance can be found there, such as a flat-headed mayfly, water penny, stonefly, hellgrammite, net-spinning caddisfly, blackfly larvae, and rhyacophilia caddisfly. children.label: D6 Famous Lakes
children.description: The  Caspian  Sea is the largest lake in the entire world both by surface area and by volume, with a  surface area of 371,000 km^2 and a volume of 78,200 km^3. Its origin class is tectonic. It formed when tectonic plate movements isolated itself from the Tethys Ocean. Its salinity class is mesosaline, and while the south is warm monomictic, the north Caspian sea is Dimictic. The largest freshwater lake is Lake Superior, with a surface area  of 82,100 km^2  and a volume of 12,100 km^3. It is a dimictic, freshwater lake. The oldest, deepest, and largest freshwater lake by volume is Lake Baikal. It is 25-30 million years old, and is 1,642 meters deep! It is also 23,615 km^3, and has a surface area of 31,722  km^2. It holds  20% of the world’s unfrozen surface fresh waters, and because of its age,  80% of its species can be found nowhere else on Earth. It is a dimictic freshwater lake. ±The Aral Sea is an extreme example of human-caused freshwater disaster. It is located between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. It dried up when  the river that “fed” was diverted. In turn, it went from mesosaline to hypersaline. It’s located in a tectonic depression, and it is meromictic.

children.label: D7.1 Diatoms
children.description: Overview: Diatoms are glass-like cells with a wall made of silica. They are the base of a food web. They are the first algae to bloom in early spring when there are nutrients and light, and are indicators of good water quality. As I already said, their cell wall is made of silica. They create a chalky white powder called diatomaceous earth. WHen they die in massive numbers in lakes, their glass shells sink and pile up on the lakebed. If a rock has a thick layer of diatom shells, it suggests that the lake once had a very high biological productivity. They bloom in the spring and die in the summer. This is because the mixing during the spring means the diatoms can float and stay alive, and they are able to outcompete everyone in nutrients and such. In the summer, the lake stratisfies, and the diatoms sink, except for some diatoms like Asterionella, which floats because of its star shape. During a phosphorus pollution, the diatoms can suck up all the dissolved silica. Once the silica is gone, the diatoms are gone as well. This is called the “Silica Depletion Hypothosis.” Diatoms are graded on a “tolence scale,” 0 being clean and 5 being polluted. A “canary,” or a Meridion Circulare, is a fan-shaped diatom with a score of 0-1. The “cockroach,” or a Nitzschia Palea, is a boat-shaped diatom with a score of 4-5. Additionally, eunotia is an indicated or acid rain.

children.label: D7.2 Cyanobacteria / Blue-Green Algae
children.description: These are the “scum” of the lake. These aren’t “algae,” but photosynthetic bacteria. These can cause harmful algal blooms when a lake gets excess nutrients like phosphorus and nitrogen. They live in nutrient-rich conditions, and can outcompete algae like diatoms by using different nutrient sources. Additionally, they aren’t a good food source, making them essentially useless. Even if you remove all the algae, they can form akinetes, or thick-walled, resilient spores.

children.label: E1.2 Transpiration
children.description: Transpiration is the release of water vapor from plants through their pores, or stomata. Combined with  evaporation, it is called evapotranspiration.

children.label: E1.3 Condensation
children.description: This happens when water vapor changes into water. Clouds can form and stuff. In order for water vapor to condense, however, they need tiny solid particles, or aerosols, to cling onto. They are typically less than 1/1000th of a millimeter, and can include dust, sea salt, smoke , soot, pollen, volcanic ash, and sulfate aerosols from industrial pollution. Aerosols help the condensation process. Without aerosols, water vapor wold need to have 400% relative humidity, but with aerosols, it is only 100%. Also, the lapse rate is the speed of which the air cools off as the water vapor  moves  upwards.  The Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate is the rate at which dry air cools as it rises, which is around 10 celsius per 1000 meters. The Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate is the rate at which saturated air cools as it rises, which is around 5-7 celsius per 1000 meters. Finally, the Dew Point is the temperature in which condensation begins.

children.label: E1.4 Percipitation
children.description: Precipitation is any water that falls from the air to earth. It can fall via rain, snow, hail, or misc. The bergeron process occurs in clouds that exist below freezing. The water vapor requires less energy to deposit (change from gas to solid) on ice crystals than into liquid. Because of that, ice crystals suck up water vapor and grow fast and fall. If the surface is cold, they fall as snow. If they pass through warm air, they melt into rain. The Collision-Coalescence applies to warmer clouds above freezing. Tiny cloud droplets, around 20 microns, are bumped arounds. If two collide, they Coalesce, or stick together, forming a larger droplet that falls faster an collides with even more droplets.A droplet must grow to at least 3000 microns, or 3 mm, to fall down. This process, however, is very flow and requires the cloud to be at least 1000 meters deep to give droplets enough time to grow. We can measure rain from the sky in two ways: satellite and weather RADAR. satellite measures infrared or microwave radiation of the cloud tops. The colder a cloud top is, the thicker the clouds are, and the more potential rain there is. Weather radars send out a pulse of microwave energy, which bounces off raindrops and returns to receive. Intensity tells amount of rain falling. NOTE: 90% of  this precipitation returns to oceans, only 10% falls on land Now let’s go over some types of precipitation. children.label: E2.1 Overland Flow
children.description: Overland flow is water flow over land. That is, they don’t go into the soil. There are two mechanisms for over land flow: Hortonion Overland Flow, named after Robert E. Horton in the 1930s, is also known as Infiltration Excess Overland Flow. When rainfall intensity exceeds soil infiltration capacity, some water is left unabsorbed by the soil; the soil cannot absorb water fast enough. This water then pools and flows over surface. Dunne Overland Flow, or saturation overland flow, named after Thomas Dunne in the 1960-1970s occurs when the soil becomes completely saturated with water. That is to say, it is completely “full” with water, it cannot absorb any more. Thus, any more water just flows over the surface. Though fancy shamncy Hewlett & Hibeert, in 1967, created the variable source concept. This essentially says that only saturated areas near water wuch as in streams contribute, and tehse saturated areas expand and contract during storms. It essentially says that the runoff contribution area is dynamic (planet). This concept is the foundation of modern hydrology.

children.label: E2.2 Soil Moisture

It occurs when water enters the soil surface from above, also known as infiltration, and moves down through soil into deeper areas, a process known as percolation. The amount of water that a soil can hold onto after excess water drains is called field capacity. When there is so much excess water that plants cannot suck up water because the water is held too tightly by soil particles, the soil has surpassed the permanent wilting point. Finally, the available water is the water that is available for plants to use. Also, different types of soil will give up water more easily, and thus have a smaller field capacity. Soils with smaller field capacity may need more irrigation. Different plants require different soil moistness as well. For example,e cacti and succulents can survive in nearly 0% moisture for long periods. Rice paddies prefer to have 100% saturation (flooded). Lawn grass and crops optimally sit at around 30% moisture by weight. Speaking of plants, the root zone is the upper layer of soil of which plants roots grow and extract water, and can extend to the upper 200 meters below surface, though usually it is 1-2 meters. Finally, hydrophobic soil is soil that repels water instead of absorbing it. This is because the soil particles are coated with waxy organic compounds from decomposing plant matter, which can be caused by wildfires vaporizing organic compounds that condense on soil particles. Anyways, water landing on hydrophobic soil bead up instead of soaking in.

children.label: F2.1 Physical Weathering
children.description: Physical weathering, or mechanical weathering, is the breakdown of rock into smaller pieces without changing its chemical composition. There are 6 or 7 (AHAHAHAHAHA *wheeeeeeeeeeeeeze* OH HO HO TEEHEEhee hee. tee.) main types of physical weathering. Frost wedging occurs when water seeps into cracks in rocks and freezes, thus expanding by around 9%. This exerts pressure in the crack walls and makes the crack a little bigger. This repeats until rock fragments break off. Haloclasty, halo meaning salt and clast meaning broken, occurs when saltwater enters the cracks in rocks. When the water evaporates, the salt crystals are left behind. When salt crystals grow, they excerpt immense pressure, up to 300 MPa,, on the rock walls, and the rock disintegrates. Honey Disaggregation occurs when honey, or other sugary substances, seep into rock pores. When honey crystallizes, it expands, forcing the rock cracks apart. Exfoliation/Onion-skin weathering occurs when something causes a rock to feel immense pressure, such as being under a lot of heavy rocks. When that pressure is released, it can create cracks forming parallel to the surface. The outer layers then peel off like onion skins. Abrasion occurs when rock particles scrap against other rocks during transport in rivers, wearing down surfaces. (Also found in A5. Sediments) Root Wedging occurs when plant roots grow into rock cracks, expand, and split the rock. Finally, lsat but not least, Getting murdered in the first degree is when ethan grabs a rock and brutally beats it with a hammer. children.label: F2.2 Chemical Weathering
children.description: Chemical weathering is like the wearing down of rocks by means of a chemical change. There are 3 main subtypes: Carbonation: when rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, it forms carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which can dissolve carbonate rocks like limestone or dolomite. This is actually how karst topography is formed. Oxidation occurs when oxygen combines with minerals and causes the mineral to rust. Yay. Hydrolysis occurs when water reacts chemical with minerals. Hydrogen ions from water can replace other ions in the mineral. For example, Silicate minerals like feldspar can break down in to clay minerals. Organic Acids secreted by lichen and fungi can dissolve rock. Spheroidal Weathering is also quite important. It occurs because chemical weathering affects different parts of a rock in different ways. If a rock is shaped like a cube, it will sand down the corners first before affecting the rest, creating a sphere. Then, it will affect the other sphere moer than the inside, creating an onion-layer-like thingy, similar to onion-skin weathering.

children.label: F3.1 Definition and Anatomy
children.description: Permofrost is ground that remains below freezing for at least two consecutive years. It is defined by temperature, not by the presence of ice. Permafrost actually covers 24% of the exposed land surface in the North Hemisphere, such as in the Arctic regions or high-altitude mountainous regions. It has two main layers: the active layer and the permafrost. The active layer sits above the permafrost and can melt in the summer and freeze in the winter. It can vary from a few centimeters deep to several meters. Below the permafrost is the talik, which stays unfrozen all year long.

children.label: F3.2 Pingos
children.description: Pingos are hill-like mounds of ice covered by soil. There are two types of pingos: open-system and closed-system. A closed-system pingo is trapped in a closed body of a water. Usually, in a drying lake. They form in 5 steps: There is a lake in a cold place The lake begins to dry up The newly exposed ground freezes for the winter, expanding and pushing the remaining water into the center The water in the center also freezes This freezing pushes dirt above it upward, making a hill. These are more commonly found in flat, lowland areas, old lake beds, river deltas. An open-system pingohas a continuous supply from a groundwater aquifer. They also form in 5 steps: Water flows beneath the permafrost The water is under high artesian pressure, it is being pushed upwards The water finds a weak spot in the permafrost The pressurized water rises and freezes near the surface. The ice pushes the dirt and rock upward into a hill. These are commonly found at valley bottoms, mountain footslopes, and hilly areas, and are also rarer than closed-system pingos. Why do pingos matter? I mean they trap a lot of methane and are a good indicator of permafrost? Ok go away.

children.label: F3.3 Solifluction
children.description: Solifluction is the slow, downslope flow of water-saturated soil over permafrost, creating wave-like lobes, as shown on the right. This happens when the active layer melts and slides slowly downhill because of gravity. Note that this only happens in the summer because anytime else the active layer is frozen.

children.label: F3.4 Permafrost Melting

Finally, what I described in the first sentence was total porosity, but effective porosity, in which void space is any space water can reach, is more useful. Related to porosity we have specific yield and retention. Specific yield is the amount of water that can be drained out via the natural forces of gravity Permeability Permeability is the ability of soil or rock to transmit water. It is dependent on how connected the pore spaces in the soil are. Sand/gravel have a very high permeability. Silt has medium, clay has low, because the pores are tiny and poorly connected, and hydrophobic soil is extremely low. Soil Structure Soil structure is the arrangement of soil particles into aggregates, or clumps. There are 6 main structure types: Granular, which are small, rounded clumps. These are good for plants. Blotchy, block-shaped clumps, common in subsoil. Prismatic, which contains vertical columns. These are common in clay-rich soils. Platy, which has thin, flat layers. Water doesn’t flow well through these. Single-grain, which has no clumping, such as sand, allowing water to flow well. Massive, with no structure, such as clay. Soil Color Soil color can indicate what minerals are present and what processes occurred within the soil. If  soil is brown or dark, that means there is organic matter and the soil is fertile. If it is red/orange, that means there is iron inside that is oxidized, and the soil is well-drained. If it is gray/blue, it means the iron inside has reduced. It had waterlogged, and had poor drainage. If it is white/light, that means it includes calcium carbonate, salt, or silica. Soil pH Uhhh like how acidic the soil is. If soil has <6 pH, then it is acidic. There may be aluminum toxicity. 6-7 pH (AHAHAHHAHA), then it is slightly acidic. This acidic range is preferred by plants. 7-8 pH, then it is slightly basic. Most plants tolerate this range. >8 pH, then it is basic/alkaline. There is calcium carbonate, and there may be lack of nutrient. Soil Horizons/Layers These are…layers…in soil. Horizon Definition O Organic Layer. This is the topmost layer, filled with leaves, litter, and humus. A This is the topsoil, a mixture of organic stuff and minerals. This has a dark color. E Eluviation layer. This is full of clay and minerals, and has a light color. B This is the subsoil, a collection of minerals such as clay, iron, and calcium. C This is the parent material, full of partially weathered rock fragments. R The bottom is bedrock, which is unweathered solid rock;.

children.label: G1 What is Karst?
children.description: Karst Landscapes are formed by the dissolving of soluble bedrock by water. Most of the time this soluble stuff is bedrock, but it can also include dolomite, gypsum and salt. This stuff is dissolved by infiltrating rainwater, and creates cracks that widen. The surface collapses, and karst topography forms.  They cover around 10-15% of the earth’s land surface.

children.description: Solution Caves begin to form when a limestone/dolomite plateau pushed upward via tectonic activities. As it lifts, it creates horizontal bedding planes and vertical joints. Anyways, rain, when heading down, passes through CO2 in the oxygen, turning it slightly acidic. And then, it reaches the floor and penetrates it *vine boom.* The slightly acidic rainwater flows through the bedding planes and joints,  creating clints and grikes. Lemme draw a picture holdup…ok done. So like after rainwater penetrates *vine boom.* The large gaps formed by the erosion of rainwater are called grikes, while the uniform uneroded limestone is called clints. It starts in its Hairline phase, which lasts 10,000 - 100,000 years, just to get microscopic hairline-sized tubes. Then, the conduit phase occurs, occurs when a crack (mmm) widens to 1-5 mm, and the flow of water turns into turbulent water. Then, air-filled phase occurs in which tectonic uplift pushes everything up, and water drains out. Eventually, they carve them into solution caves. Actually, there are two types of solution caves depending on where you are looking. Caves in the vadose zone, or above the water table, have water moving down. There are huge vertical shafts, deep slots, and twisting rocky passages. In the phreatic zone, below the water table, the area is already filled with water, and contains round, smooth tunnels. Note that solution caves form fastest at the water table, because acidic water can combine with already existing groundwater to MASS DESTROY MUAHEHE.
